claims.text: Tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys will exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition over the typical temper-embrittlement temperature range.
Tungsten-based RHEAs will undergo less embrittlement than conventional steels.
High configurational entropy and multi-principal-element design cause reduced temper embrittlement.
The proposed initial material is a cast W-Ta-Cr-V-Mo refractory high-entropy alloy in near-equimolar proportions.
Composition adjustment can ensure a stable single- or dual-phase structure in the proposed alloy.
The typical temper-embrittlement temperature range is approximately 200–600 °C.
A multi-principal-element matrix reduces detrimental impurity segregation.
A multi-principal-element matrix stabilizes the microstructure against embrittling transformations.
Refractory high-entropy alloys exhibit sluggish diffusion of their constituent elements.
High configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion reduce the usual temper-embrittlement mechanism.
Reduced temper embrittlement allows ductility to return after annealing at temperatures above the embrittlement range.
Tungsten-based RHEAs will show a pronounced ductile–brittle–ductile transition while retaining more ductility than conventional temper-embrittled alloys.
Conventional low-alloy steels undergo severe temper embrittlement in the 200–600 °C range.
Inadequate compositional homogeneity or excessive porosity may reduce the alloy's resistance to embrittlement.
Transition temperatures and the magnitude of ductility recovery depend on small composition changes and heat-treatment protocols.
Refractory HEAs are multicomponent systems containing several principal elements.
Configurational entropy can promote solid-solution formation in high-entropy alloys.
